message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This audit is based on the full appointment record for six months, all 24,860 booked appointments, rather than a sample, so the figures are complete and the rates are exact. We were careful with definitions, separating genuine DNAs from late cancellations, and we costed the impact in clinical time so the Division can see what is at stake: around £80,900 every six months. The most useful finding is about reminder calls. Patients who received a call had a DNA rate of 6.0% against 12.5% for those who did not, which shows that a simple, low-tech intervention the service already uses more than halves missed appointments. Extending it is the obvious, practical step, and it uses staff and processes that are already in place, so it does not need new funding. We also identified concrete, fixable weaknesses in the discharge policy and in refilling late cancellations. I believe the recommendations are proportionate and will bring the service within target.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.
</document>
response:
# Review: not ready to go to the Director yet

The arithmetic checks out, but the main recommendation rests on a causal claim the data can't support, and its "no additional cost" claim is contradicted by the memo's own figures. There is also a definitional inconsistency in Finding 1.

## Must fix before it goes

**1. The "no additional cost" claim doesn't hold (Rec 1)**
- Using your own 4 minutes per call, the 17,060 appointments not currently called need about 656 extra calls a week. That is roughly 44 extra reception hours a week, more than one full-time post, on top of the ~20 hours already spent.
- Section 3 also says calls are made "where time allows," which suggests reception is already stretched.
- Unanswered calls and retries cost time too, so this is a floor.
- Either cost this (staff time, or a different channel such as automated calls or texts) or drop "at no additional cost." This is the point the Director is most likely to challenge.

**2. The 6.0% vs 12.5% comparison doesn't show that calls "more than halve" DNAs**
- A call counts as "received" only if the patient answered *and confirmed they'd attend*. That selects for engaged, reachable patients. Patients who didn't answer, or who said they wouldn't come, sit in the "no reminder" group, which inflates its DNA rate.
- Staff called "where time allows," so who got called probably wasn't random.
- The groups may also differ in appointment type, site, or time of day. New assessments DNA at 6.6% against 11.8% for follow-ups, so a skew toward new patients alone would narrow the gap.
- The gap is real, but the likely effect of calls is smaller than 6.5 points. The statements "shown to more than halve DNAs" (Section 7) and "would bring the service well within its 8% target" (Section 3) are not supported.
- Fixes:
  - Break Table 2 down by appointment type and site.
  - Report how many calls were attempted but unanswered.
  - Describe the finding as an association.
  - Propose a staged rollout at one site, with a comparison, so the effect can be measured before committing resources.

**3. Finding 1 contradicts Section 1**
- Section 1 says late cancellations are reported separately and excluded from DNAs. The 10.5% figure and the £80,900 are consistent with that (2,610 DNAs).
- Finding 1 then says the 10.5% includes late cancellations, which "we classify as DNAs." If they were included, the rate would be (2,610 + 1,140) / 24,860 = 15.1%.
- Remove the parenthetical from Finding 1 and keep the definition consistent. Say explicitly that late cancellations are a further loss not included in the £80,900.

**4. The conclusion overreaches**
- "Should bring the DNA rate below target within six months" has no calculation behind it. Recs 2 and 3 have no estimated effect on DNAs at all.
- Rec 2 adds a review step, which may reduce discharges rather than DNAs. Rec 3 targets late cancellations, which are outside the 10.5%.
- Either show a range (for example, the DNA rate if calls achieve one-quarter, one-half, or all of the observed gap) or soften this to "may contribute to."

## Should fix

- **Rec 3 has no cost or feasibility statement.** An automated text offer needs system capability or a licence. Say whether it exists, and what it costs.
- **Rec 2 isn't linked to the DNA target.** 104 of 160 patients were discharged (65%). Say what the intended effect on DNAs is, or present it as a governance fix rather than a DNA-reduction measure.
- **The cost figure is a capacity cost, not cash.** £80,900 is the value of unused clinical time. Say so, and note that it is only recoverable if slots can be refilled.
- **Follow-up DNAs are the largest problem (2,200 of 2,610).** Staff attribute many to patients who feel better. Consider whether a reminder call addresses that, or whether a discharge or "planned end of treatment" conversation would do more.

## On the author's summary

"Complete data, so the rates are exact" is true for the rates but not for what they mean. Having every appointment removes sampling error. It doesn't remove the selection problem in the reminder comparison. "Does not need new funding" should be removed unless the staffing gap in point 1 is resolved.

## Suggested revised headline

> Patients who answered and confirmed a reminder call missed 6.0% of appointments against 12.5% for others. Part of this gap is probably selection, but it is large enough to justify extending calls. We recommend a costed, staged rollout with measurement.

With that change, costs added to Recs 1 and 3, and the Finding 1 correction, the memo would be ready.
